name: Distribution shift and online recalibration. Core: Gupta & Ramdas (2023), 'Online Platt Scaling with Calibeating' (ICML 2023, PMLR 202:12182-12204; arXiv:2305.00070). Theory companion: Foster & Hart (2023), '"Calibeating": Beating Forecasters at Their Own Game' (Theoretical Economics 18(4):1441-1474; arXiv:2209.04892). Antecedent: Kuleshov & Ermon (2017), online recalibration by binning + hedging of a black-box forecaster.
type: method family (post-hoc online recalibration under distribution drift: Online Platt Scaling (OPS) via online logistic regression, plus calibeating wrappers TOPS (tracking) and HOPS (hedging); beta-scaling extension OBS/TOBS/HOBS)
url: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00070 ; PMLR: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/gupta23c.html ; HTML: https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2305.00070 ; Code: https://github.com/aigen/df-posthoc-calibration (folder 'Online Platt Scaling with Calibeating') ; Foster & Hart: https://doi.org/10.3982/TE5330 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04892
year: 2023 (arXiv v1 28 Apr 2023, v3 16 Aug 2023; ICML 2023). Foster & Hart: arXiv Sep 2022, Theoretical Economics Nov 2023. Code repo last pushed 2023-10-20.
authors: Chirag Gupta, Aaditya Ramdas (Carnegie Mellon University). Foster & Hart: Dean P. Foster, Sergiu Hart. Code maintained by Chirag Gupta (GitHub 'aigen').
popularity: Semantic Scholar (retrieved 2026-10-17): Gupta & Ramdas 2023 = 12 citations (1 influential); Foster & Hart 'Calibeating' = 23 citations. GitHub aigen/df-posthoc-calibration = 41 stars, MIT license. A niche but well-founded line of work; not a mainstream forecasting tool.
peer_review_status: peer-reviewed (ICML 2023 conference paper; Theoretical Economics journal paper). Both also on arXiv.
target_type: Not an air-alert application. Generic binary classification / probability forecast y in {0,1} with a black-box score f(x) in [0,1]. Recalibration does not change the target, so the onset-vs-state choice and our at-risk mask (CLAUDE.md Target) are fixed upstream. Note: a recalibrator fitted on a state target would happily learn the high base rate of 'already under alert' rows, so the mask must be applied BEFORE any online update, not only at scoring.
target_definition: Generic: Y_t = 1 if the event occurs at stream step t; forecast p_t issued before Y_t is revealed, then Y_t is observed and the recalibrator updates (one point per step, labels revealed immediately). For our project the event is 'a new alert starts in (t, t+H]', H = 1 h, per oblast-hour, and labels mature only at t+H (D-021 label-maturity rule), which the paper's protocol does not model.
spatial_unit: Not applicable (tabular UCI/Kaggle datasets and synthetic streams). For us the natural choices are a single pooled recalibrator across the 24 units, one per group (Kyiv City / frontline / rear), or a per-unit intercept; per-unit 2-parameter OPS would be noisy for quiet rear oblasts.
at_risk_masking: Not addressed (no at-risk concept). Applied to our task, masked rows (already under alert at t, gap hours D-013) must be excluded from BOTH the prediction set and the online update stream, exactly as for the rolling recent-rate baseline (unmasked rows s in [t-14d, t-H]).
data_sources: Real data (Sec. 4, Table 2): Bank marketing (sort-by Age), Credit default (Sex), Customer churn (Location), Fetal health (Acceleration). T_train = 1000 (626 for Fetal health), T_cal = 1000 (300), window W = 500 (100). Synthetic (Sec. 1.2, Figs. 3/10/11): 1-D/48-D logistic streams of ~6000 points with covariate drift (rotating principal direction), label drift (P(Y=1) changing over time) and regression-function drift. Appendix D: a covariate-free rain-forecasting illustration showing hedging collapses to climatology (~0.35) [uncertain: dataset/location not re-checked].
data_source_variant: Not applicable (no air-alert data). Drift on real data is INDUCED by sorting on one covariate with small noise, i.e. a constructed covariate shift, not a naturally occurring regime change such as the 2026-09-07 yellow/red reform.
preprocessing: Base-model scores clipped to f(x) in [0.01, 0.99] for the regret theorem (Thm 2.1); the logit of the score is the single pseudo-feature for online logistic regression. Real-data streams are created by sorting rows on a chosen covariate after adding noise from {-1, 0, 1}; the i.i.d. control is a random shuffle. 100 repetitions per real-data experiment.
known_label_artefacts: Not applicable to air alerts (no duplicates, gaps, standing alerts or 30-min artefacts). Method-level artefacts worth noting: (1) Fixed-width epsilon-bins (epsilon = 0.1, m = 10) are used for both the calibeating wrappers and the CE metric. At our hourly onset base rates in the official regime (a few percent), nearly all forecasts fall in [0, 0.1), so TOPS would degenerate to one running mean for almost all rows; this is the same instability CORP documents for reliability diagrams. (2) Covariate-free hedging (Appendix D) can look perfectly calibrated while being uninformative (converges to climatology). (3) The CE metric itself is a binned estimate and inherits bin-choice sensitivity (paper shows epsilon = 0.05 / 0.2 give qualitatively the same ranking).
model_family: Post-hoc recalibration layered on a frozen base model. (1) OPS: the Platt map m_{a,b}(f) = sigmoid(a * logit(f) + b) with (a_t, b_t) learned by ONLINE logistic regression on the stream (d = 2). Implementation uses Online Newton Step (ONS) with gamma = 0.1, rho = 100 (A_0 = rho I), projection onto K = {||(a,b)||_2 <= 100}, initialisation (a_1, b_1) = (1, 0), i.e. the identity map = the uncalibrated base model. Hyperparameters were fixed once, not tuned per dataset. Alternatives compared in Table 1: OGD, ONS, AIOLI, Aggregating Algorithm; FTL is O(T^2) so a windowed refit (WPS, refit every ~100 steps on the last W points) is used as a comparator. Regret vs best Platt model in an l2-ball of radius B: ONS R_T <= 2(e^B + 10B) log T + 1; AIOLI R_T <= 22 B log(BT). (2) Calibeating (after Foster & Hart 2023): TOPS = for each epsilon-bin of the OPS forecast, output the running mean of past outcomes whose OPS forecast fell in that bin (bin midpoint if empty); HOPS = a separate Foster (1999) randomized hedging forecaster inside each bin. (3) Beta scaling: sigmoid(a log f + b log(1-f) + c) (b = -a recovers Platt), learned online by ONS in R^3 (rho = 25, init (1,1,0)), with tracking/hedging variants TOBS/HOBS. Baselines: base model (BM), fixed Platt scaling fitted once on T_cal (FPS), windowed Platt scaling (WPS), windowed histogram binning (WHB, Appendix A.3).
features: One pseudo-feature: logit(f(x_t)) from a frozen base model, plus intercept (Platt); log f and log(1-f) plus intercept (beta scaling). Base models: random forest (sklearn, n_estimators = 1000) on real data; logistic regression on synthetic data (48-dim sinusoidal featurisation for covariate drift). For us the analogue is the frozen LightGBM output (src/model.py) as f, and the recalibrator never sees the raw features, so it cannot add feature leakage; its only new information is past matured labels.
external_feature_timing: Not applicable (no external covariates). Timing issue that DOES matter for us: the paper assumes the label of step t is revealed before step t+1. With 24 units per forecast hour and H-hour label windows, a causal implementation must (a) predict all 24 unit-rows at t with parameters frozen before t, then (b) update only with rows whose label window (s, s+H] ended by t, i.e. s <= t - H. Updating within an hour across units in arbitrary order would leak same-hour onsets (mass attacks hit many oblasts in the same hour).
ablation_design: Methods are compared on identical streams (same base model, same T_train / T_cal split, same 100 repetitions), with an i.i.d. (shuffled) control vs drifting (sorted) version of the same data. This is a clean same-sample design. Sensitivity analysis on the only calibeating hyperparameter (epsilon in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}, Appendix A.3).
split_scheme: Chronological stream: first T_train points train the base model (frozen thereafter, no refit on the stream); next T_cal points fit FPS and warm up the windowed methods; the remaining points form the online test stream, where each method predicts then updates. Online methods update every step; WPS/WBS refit on a sliding window of W points. No purge needed because labels are instantaneous.
metrics: Sharpness SHP (eq. 14, the observed refinement-type quantity: higher is better) and l1 calibration error CE over epsilon-bins (eq. 17). Synthetic experiments use the TRUE conditional probabilities for CE and accuracy over time windows (e.g. t = 5501-6000). Brier score enters the theory via the Foster-Hart decomposition Brier = calibration + refinement; TOPS/HOPS keep refinement (sharpness) within O(epsilon) of OPS while improving calibration. No ROC-AUC or PR-AUC (recalibration by a monotone map leaves AUC unchanged; calibeating's binning can only coarsen ranking).
unit_of_metric: Pooled over the stream (or over time windows of the stream); means over 100 repetitions. No per-group breakdown.
baseline_strength: Baselines: uncalibrated base model (BM), fixed Platt scaling (FPS), windowed Platt scaling (WPS), windowed histogram binning (WHB), and windowed beta scaling (WBS). Under drift, BM and FPS are the worst non-calibeating methods; OPS has the lowest CE among non-calibeating methods; TOPS is best overall 'by a margin' with sharpness losses of about 0.005 or less. On i.i.d. data the gaps shrink; WHB beats OPS/OBS on i.i.d. data and is mixed under drift. WPS is described as much worse than OPS/TOPS on synthetic drift. No comparison with a simple rolling-base-rate forecaster, which is our strongest bar (rolling recent-rate, D-021).
calibration: The paper IS a calibration method. Calibration is fitted ONLINE on the evaluation stream itself, but causally (predict-then-update), so it is legitimate out-of-sample. Fixed Platt (FPS) is fitted once on a held-out calibration slice, the analogue of our M4 rule (Platt on validation if validation ECE > 0.02; our official run gave ECE = 0.0123, decision 'none', reports/official/calibrator.json). Calibration quality is reported as binned CE; no reliability diagrams in the CORP sense. Guarantees: OPS has only a REGRET guarantee relative to the best fixed Platt map (no absolute calibration bound); TOPS has a sharpness guarantee SHP(TOPS) >= SHP(OPS) - epsilon - epsilon^2/4 - (log T + 1)/(epsilon T) but no calibration guarantee; HOPS (randomized) has E[CE] <= epsilon/2 + 2 sqrt(1/(epsilon^2 T)) even for adversarial outcome sequences.
calibration_under_drift: Central topic. Drift types studied: covariate drift, label (base-rate) drift, regression-function drift. Under label drift (Fig. 10, t = 5500-6000) accuracy/CE go from base 59.38% / 0.42 to OPS 92.82% / 0.049; covariate drift (Fig. 3, t = 5501-6000) 23.60% / 0.64 -> 87.76% / 0.13; regression-function drift (Fig. 11) 44.39% / 0.34 -> 51.43% / 0.049. A pure base-rate shift is exactly what the Platt intercept b_t absorbs, so OPS behaves like an online calibration-in-the-large correction plus an online slope correction. Our own new-regime transfer table (reports/new_regime/transfer.csv, API 2026-09-13 -> 2026-10-12, any-level target, 7,146 at-risk rows, low_n flagged) shows exactly this pattern: the frozen model UNDER-predicts (mean predicted 0.222 vs observed 0.264, -4.2 pp overall; Kyiv City -12.3 pp, frontline -6.7 pp, rear -3.4 pp), keeps within-unit AUC 0.666 vs 0.485 for recent-rate, yet loses on Brier (BSS vs recent-rate = -0.032). That is a 'discrimination preserved, scale wrong' signature that an online intercept/slope recalibration targets. [Interpretation, not tested: OPS on the frozen model would likely close most of that Brier gap.]
uncertainty_of_gain: Real-data results are averaged over 100 random repetitions (randomness from noise in sorting/shuffling and the HOPS randomisation) and plotted with variability across runs [uncertain: whether error bars or standard deviations are shown on every figure was not re-checked]. No formal test of skill differences (no Diebold-Mariano, no block bootstrap). Theoretical bounds are worst-case (adversarial) and hold in expectation for HOPS.
regime_coverage: Synthetic smooth drifts and induced covariate shift by sorting; no real-world abrupt regime change. Nothing comparable to the Jan-2025 drone surge, the 2025 raion/hromada reform or the Sep-2026 yellow/red reform. The method's online adaptivity is relative to the best FIXED Platt map over the whole stream (static regret); the authors list adaptive/strongly-adaptive regret on recent data (Hazan & Seshadhri 2009; Zhang et al. 2018) as future work, which is what an abrupt reform would need.
leakage_handling: Causal by construction: each forecast uses only (a_t, b_t) learned from steps before t, and the base model is frozen after T_train, so no future label enters a prediction. Nothing to purge because labels are instantaneous. What the paper does NOT cover and we must add: (1) label maturity with H-hour windows (update only with rows s <= t - H, the D-021 rule already used by recent-rate); (2) simultaneous rows (24 units at the same t: batch predict, then batch update); (3) masked rows (at-risk, gap hours) excluded from updates; (4) the recalibrator state at the frozen cut-off (2026-07-27) must be initialised from validation or identity, never warmed up on test labels before the first test forecast; (5) a truncation test for the recalibrated predictor (CLAUDE.md test_leakage.py): truncating the stream after t must not change p_t. Calibeating tracking means are also causal (past outcomes only).
test_window_hygiene: Hyperparameters (ONS gamma = 0.1, rho = 100, K radius 100, init (1,0); epsilon = 0.1) were set once and reported as untuned across all datasets, which is the right posture for a pre-registered extra row. Results are fully reproducible from notebooks (fixed randomisation). No notion of a single-look final test; the stream is evaluated in full each time.
headline_results: (1) OPS, online logistic regression on logit(f) with ONS, adapts to covariate, label and regression-function drift and has logarithmic regret vs the best Platt map: ONS R_T <= 2(e^B + 10B) log T + 1. (2) Under synthetic drift, OPS sharply improves on the frozen base model (label drift: CE 0.42 -> 0.049, accuracy 59.38% -> 92.82%; covariate drift: CE 0.64 -> 0.13). (3) On four real datasets with induced drift, OPS has the lowest CE among non-calibeating methods, fixed Platt (FPS) and the base model are worst, and TOPS (OPS + tracking calibeating) is best in every scenario, losing at most ~0.005 sharpness. On shuffled (i.i.d.) data the gaps shrink and TOPS still wins. (4) HOPS gives an adversarial calibration guarantee E[CE] <= epsilon/2 + 2 sqrt(1/(epsilon^2 T)) at a small sharpness cost. (5) Online beta scaling (OBS) beats OPS and WBS; TOBS is best in each plot. (6) Foster & Hart: any forecaster can be 'calibeaten' (made calibrated while keeping its refinement score), deterministically for the tracking version. No result is reported against a rolling base-rate forecaster, so 'beats naive baselines' is only shown vs the frozen base model and fixed/windowed Platt.
code_available: Yes. https://github.com/aigen/df-posthoc-calibration (MIT, 41 stars, last push 2023-10-20, not actively maintained). Folder 'Online Platt Scaling with Calibeating' holds sec_1_*_drift_1d.ipynb (synthetic drift), sec_4_experiments_core.py/_run.ipynb (real data), beta_scaling_experiments.py, eps_core.py (epsilon sensitivity), app_a3_hb_experiments_* (histogram binning) and calibration.py/utils.py. The authors state all figures reproduce exactly. For this project no new dependency is needed: ONS for d = 2 is ~20 lines of NumPy (2x2 matrix update + projection), and TOPS is a running per-bin mean. Adding the repo as a dependency would need Oleksandr's approval (CLAUDE.md).
takeaways_for_project:
1) Our rolling recent-rate baseline (D-021: (k + 10 p_unit)/(n + 10) over unmasked rows in [t-14d, t-H]) is already an online, intercept-only recalibration of a constant forecaster. OPS is the principled generalisation: an online intercept AND slope applied to the frozen model's logit. This gives the README a clean story for why recent-rate is hard to beat after drift: it adapts its level every hour, while the frozen model (and fixed Platt, FPS) cannot. The paper confirms empirically that frozen and fixed-Platt forecasters are the worst under drift.
2) The new-regime transfer result (reports/new_regime/transfer.csv) fits the 'discrimination preserved, scale wrong' case OPS is designed for: frozen model mean predicted 0.222 vs observed 0.264 (-4.2 pp; Kyiv City -12.3 pp), within-unit AUC 0.666 vs 0.485 for recent-rate, BSS vs recent-rate -0.032. The D-015(d) conclusion can then say, as a hypothesis, 'recalibration (not necessarily retraining) is the first remedy', and cite OPS as the method. State the measured numbers as facts and the OPS remedy as an untested hypothesis (D-015 amended).
3) RULE CONFLICT, needs Oleksandr: running OPS on API data is fitting 2 parameters on API labels, which CLAUDE.md forbids ('No training or tuning on API data'), even though it is as causal as the rolling recent-rate baseline that is allowed. Likewise, on the official test window it would be a second exception to 'baselines/model frozen', like D-021's recent-rate exception and the D-014 weekly-refit EXTRA row. If approved, report it ONLY as an extra row ('frozen model + online Platt'), never the headline.
4) If approved, pre-register the implementation exactly as in the paper to avoid test-time tuning: ONS with gamma = 0.1, rho = 100, ||(a,b)|| <= 100, init (a,b) = (1,0) (identity = the frozen model on day one), logit computed on clipped p (we already clip at 1e-6 in src/model.py; the paper's theorem assumes [0.01, 0.99]). One POOLED (a,b) across units, optionally plus a per-group intercept; per-unit slopes would be noise for quiet rear oblasts. Fix all of this in the plan before scoring (D-026 consensus, then human ratification).
5) Causality details the paper does not handle and we must: batch-predict all 24 units at t with parameters frozen before t; update only with matured rows s <= t - H (D-021); skip masked rows (at-risk at t, gap hours 2026-08-29 -> 09-02, D-013); never update within the same hour across units (mass attacks would leak). Add a truncation test to tests/test_leakage.py: p_t from the online recalibrator must be identical when the stream is cut after t.
6) Do NOT use calibeating with the paper's 10 fixed-width bins on the official regime: onset base rates of a few percent put almost all rows in [0, 0.1), so TOPS collapses to a single running mean, i.e. a worse recent-rate. If tracking is tried, use pre-registered log-spaced or quantile bins from validation, and note TOPS uses all-history bin means that adapt slowly to an abrupt reform. In the new regime (base rate ~0.26 at-risk) fixed bins are less degenerate.
7) Do NOT use HOPS (randomised hedging) for a public-facing forecast: its guarantee is in expectation over the forecaster's own coin flips, and a randomly jittered alert probability is hard to explain to users. The paper's Appendix D also shows covariate-free hedging converges to climatology, calibrated but useless; calibration alone is not the goal (Foster & Hart: judge by Brier, i.e. calibration + refinement).
8) Monotone recalibration leaves ROC-AUC unchanged, so the D-015(c) within-oblast AUC is a fair check of whether discrimination transferred, independent of any recalibration; any Brier gain from OPS is pure calibration (MCB in CORP terms). Report OPS gains as an MCB reduction against the frozen model.
9) For M6 (future work, D-016): an online recalibrator updated monthly (or hourly) from the datastore is a cheaper first response to drift than a full retrain, and fits the 'pytest before retrain' gate. The paper's static-regret guarantee is weak for abrupt reforms; a sliding-window or discounted variant (adaptive regret, cited as future work in the paper) would be the honest choice, and must be pre-registered.
best_practices: ADOPT: (a) Treat recalibration as a separate, causal layer on a frozen model, with its own leakage test, rather than retraining after every shift. (b) Initialise the online recalibrator at the identity map so that day-one predictions equal the frozen model, and fix all hyperparameters before scoring (the paper uses one untuned setting for every dataset). (c) Compare against the frozen model, fixed Platt AND a windowed/rolling competitor on the identical stream, with an i.i.d.-shuffled control to separate drift effects from generic miscalibration. (d) Judge by a proper score (Brier = calibration + refinement, Foster & Hart), not by calibration error alone. (e) Report calibration-in-the-large (mean predicted - observed) per group before and after recalibration; a base-rate shift shows up as a level offset that an online intercept absorbs. (f) Respect label delay (s <= t - H) and simultaneous units (batch updates). AVOID: (1) Fixed Platt fitted once and assumed valid after a regime change. (2) Fixed-width 0.1 bins (for calibeating or CE) at low base rates. (3) Randomised hedging forecasts in a user-facing product. (4) Treating a calibrated-but-flat forecaster (climatology-like) as success. (5) Warm-starting the recalibrator on test labels before the first scored forecast, or tuning gamma/rho/epsilon on the test or API window. (6) Calling an online-recalibrated row 'the frozen model': it is a different predictor and must be labelled as an extra row. (7) Assuming static-regret guarantees cover abrupt reforms; they compete only with the best single Platt map over the whole stream.
